Basal metabolic rate measurements conducted under controlled laboratory conditions using flow-through respirometry revealed that the Egyptian slit-faced bat maintains a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 18.76 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 18.76 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when ambient temperatures are held at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This relatively modest metabolic output, recorded from post-absorptive individuals during their inactive phase, aligns with the energy-conserving strategy typical of insectivorous bats that roost in warm, humid cave environments. The thermal conditions used in these experiments approximate the core body temperatures these animals sustain during daytime torpor, making the measured rate a reliable benchmark for the species' minimal energetic requirements.

Females give birth to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and produce exactly one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], a reproductive schedule that constrains annual fecundity to one offspring per adult female. This low reproductive output, typical of many tropical bat species, is offset by strong maternal investment in the solitary neonate, which weighs only 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams] at birth, a value consistent with the altricial condition of newborn bats and the energetic constraints on flying mothers. The altricial newborns are particularly vulnerable during the first weeks of life, and females have been observed flying while carrying their young between roosts to keep them safe from predators, a behavior that imposes additional energetic costs on the lactating mother. The maximum reproductive rate recorded for this species reflects an annual cycle tightly linked to seasonal insect abundance, at one offspring per year [Ri = at one offspring per year].

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, with females attaining a larger ultimate size than males. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches 11.5 grams [Wwi = 11.5 grams], while the ultimate wet weight for males is considerably lower at 9.7 grams [Wwi = 9.7 grams], a difference that likely reflects the energetic demands of gestation and lactation placed on reproductive females. This disparity in maximum recorded body mass is consistent across populations studied in both East and Southern Africa, suggesting a genetically fixed dimorphism rather than a purely environmental effect. The smaller male body size may confer advantages in aerial maneuverability during foraging, given that both sexes feed predominantly on Lepidoptera and Coleoptera captured in flight.

Gestation in the Egyptian slit-faced bat lasts 75 days [tg = 75 days] when development proceeds under optimal thermal conditions of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], though substantial geographic variation exists in this trait. In tropical populations, pregnancy typically spans 2 to 3 months, whereas females in temperate climates may carry their developing embryo for up to 5 months, likely reflecting the capacity for delayed implantation or adaptive metabolic suppression during cooler periods. Following parturition, the nursing pup attains nutritional independence after a weaning period of 50 days [tx = 50 days] at the same ambient temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], after which the juvenile begins consuming solid insect prey captured by the mother during nightly foraging bouts.

The species exhibits a slow life-history pace consistent with its low fecundity and relatively extended developmental periods. The maximum lifespan observed in the wild is approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years], a figure typical of slow-living bats, recorded at a mean annual temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], though individuals in captivity may exceed this duration. Sexual maturity, attained at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth], occurs when body temperatures during activity are around 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]. This combination of slow maturation and single-offspring reproduction renders the species particularly sensitive to elevated adult mortality rates, as population recovery from disturbance is inherently slow.
